Six Habits for Automation People Can Trust

October 21, 2026 Practice

This week we rebuilt how people ask the library for something it does not have yet. The work took one day, with an AI assistant doing most of the building and a person making every call that mattered. The result is a short request form, an approval step, and automation that sends, records and reports each request on its own.

The speed was not the interesting part. What made the result trustworthy was a handful of habits we kept coming back to. They apply to any automation you build with Copilot Studio, Power Automate or Microsoft 365, with or without AI help.

1. Start from what the person actually sees

Our first version showed a Request access link when a search came up empty. Read cold, that label means nothing to someone who just wanted an agent. Worse, the search is forgiving, so it almost never came up completely empty, and the link rarely appeared at all.

We changed both. Every search now ends with the same plain offer: Can't find it? Tell us what you need. No test caught this problem. Reading the page the way a first-time visitor would did.

2. Ask only what you need, only where it applies

Every form field is a small tax on the person filling it in. We removed the questions nobody used, kept the ones we genuinely need, and added branching: if your use case is not listed, the form asks you to describe it, and that answer is required. If it is listed, you never see the question.

We also ask for no customer names or customer data, and the form says so where you type. Data you never collect is data you never have to protect. Removing questions did not remove past answers; everything already submitted was kept.

3. Keep a person on the decision, automate everything after it

A request still goes to a person, who approves or declines it with one click. Everything after that click is automatic: access is granted, the email goes out, and the request is marked as sent.

Order matters here. Our first draft emailed the links before granting access, so a requester could open a link that did not work yet. Now access comes first, and the email only goes out once access is in place.

4. Silence is not success

Automation that fails quietly is worse than no automation, because everyone assumes it worked. Ours reports in both directions. When a request is sent, a confirmation arrives in Teams. When a step fails, a warning arrives instead, naming what failed, so the owner can follow up by hand.

The same principle covers work that stalls. Every morning, a reminder lists any request that has waited more than 48 hours. Nobody has to remember to check.

5. Promise only what you control

For solutions already in the library, we can usually reply within 24 to 48 hours, so the form says exactly that. A brand-new use case is different: we read every request and follow up by email, but we cannot commit to building each one. The wording reflects that difference instead of blurring it.

The same honesty decides what the library adds next. A request that comes up from several different teams is a strong signal, and those are the ones we add first.

6. Ship the smallest useful piece, and prove it

We built more than we released. Interactive features that deserve a proper review were set aside, and only the request path shipped. A smaller release is easier to review, easier to explain and easier to trust.

Before calling it done, we sent a real request through the live form and watched it travel through approval, email, the request log and the Teams confirmation. A clean build says the parts fit together. A real request is how you learn that they work.

The short version: design from the visitor's side, collect only what you need, keep a person on the decision, make the automation report its own failures, promise only what you control, and prove it with a real run before you call it done.

One Owner for a Shared Result: Fixing a Stalled Sign-In

April 11, 2026 Engineering

Version 0.6.0 of the Brainstem added an account switcher, so you can sign in with a different GitHub account without restarting it. In testing, one path did not finish: if you first signed in with an account that had no GitHub Copilot access and then switched to the right one, the sign-in screen kept waiting and never completed.

What was happening

Two parts of the Brainstem were both checking whether sign-in had finished: a small task running in the background, and the sign-in screen itself. Each could pick up the result, and once one of them did, the other found nothing left to read. When the background task got there first, the screen was left waiting.

The fix

We gave the result a single owner. The background task is now the only part that completes the sign-in, and it records the outcome, success or failure, in one place. The sign-in screen only reads that record. Nothing competes for the result, so the screen always sees it.

The pattern: when two parts of a program need the outcome of the same step, let one of them own the step and have the others read its result.

Two smaller improvements in the same release

  • If an account has no GitHub Copilot access, the sign-in screen now says so and offers to switch accounts, instead of appearing to succeed.
  • The sign-in screen stops waiting after 15 minutes, the same time a sign-in code stays valid, and asks you to start again.

Version Tracking with a Plain Text File

March 5, 2026 Engineering

The Brainstem installs with a single command, and the same command handles upgrades. To do that, the installer has to know which version you have and which version is current. We answer both with one small text file.

One file, read by everything

The file rapp_brainstem/VERSION holds the version number and nothing else. The installer reads it, the Brainstem shows it on its /version and /health pages, and people can read it too. Because there is only one place to change, the version can never disagree with itself.

How an upgrade decides what to do

When you run the install command again, it compares the version on your machine with the published one. If they match, it reports that you are already up to date and stops. If a newer version is available, it updates the Brainstem in place, keeps a copy of your own agents and settings and puts them back, and checks that everything it needs is installed. You can also ask for a specific version if you need to stay on one.

Changing the number is the last step, not the release

A new version reaches people only after it passes a staging release: automated checks, a test install of the one-line command on clean machines, and a review before it is merged. The version number records a release that has already been proven. It does not cause one.

Check your version: open http://localhost:7071/version while the Brainstem is running, or run the install command again to see whether an update is available.
